The sections studied comprise quartzites, as well as extrusive and intrusive rocks of Vepsian ( 1900-1650 Ma) and Jatulian (2300-2100 Ma) ages, which represent Svecofennian and Jatulian tectonomagmatic events respectively. However, only a minor portion of the data used for this and for the earlier compilations has been obtained from the eastern part of the Fennoscandian Shield, thus prompting the present study. In this paper we present new palaeomagnetic data for the Lake Onega region. The sections studied comprise quartzites, as well as extrusive and intrusive rocks of Vepsian ( 1900-1650 Ma) and Jatulian (2300-2100 Ma) ages, which represent Svecofennian and Jatulian tectonomagmatic events respectively. Core samples were then distributed among the participating laboratories for standard palaeomagnetic measurements. A pilot collection ( 18 samples), representative of all rock types sampled, was subjected to a variety of rock-magnetic experiments at the Institute of Physics of the Earth in Moscow. These experiments include determinations of saturation magnetization J, and saturation remanence J,, as a function of temperature, as well as AF and DC demagnetization of Jrs. The peak fields used for the latter two experiments reach 100 mT and 2000 mT respectively. In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. In the case of stronger remanence, continuous thermal demagnetization was carried out in a thermal demagnetizer incorporated in the spinner magnetometer. In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. Thermomagnetic analysis of these samples gives results that are characteristic for magnesium magnetite with a small percentage of MgO, which indicates a primary origin for this magnetite. On the other hand, petrographic and microprobe investigations have established the presence of secondary olivine-generated magnetite, which appeared during serpentinization of the Aganozero peridotites (Pisakin et al. 1992). Thermomagnetic analysis of gabbro-norites yields Jrs(T ) dependences charac- teristic of virtually pure magnetite, whereas the decay curves Jn(T ) (see Fig. 8, sample B59), in conjunction with microscopic and microprobe analyses, indicate a thermoremanent origin of the NRM in the gabbro-norites. These latter rocks, which contain so-called ‘cloudy’ plagioclase, yield results that are consistent with the formation of magnetite within such plagio- clase during the consolidation of the Burakovka intrusion (Pisakin et al. 1992).

For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

(corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S, 304.8° E, A95=8.3° ; U–Pb age of 2436± 25 Ma), the Voche-Lambina ultramaﬁcs and amphibolites (12.9 ° N, 314.1° E, A95=8.6° ; Rb–Sr age of 2198 ± 172 Ma), and the Kolvitsa peridotites and schists (44.2° N, 232.6° E, A95=5.4° ; assigned magnetization age of 1900 Ma). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S, 304.8° E, A95=8.3° ; U–Pb age of 2436± 25 Ma), the Voche-Lambina ultramaﬁcs and amphibolites (12.9 ° N, 314.1° E, A95=8.6° ; Rb–Sr age of 2198 ± 172 Ma), and the Kolvitsa peridotites and schists (44.2° N, 232.6° E, A95=5.4° ; assigned magnetization age of 1900 Ma). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S, 304.8° E, A95=8.3° ; U–Pb age of 2436± 25 Ma), the Voche-Lambina ultramaﬁcs and amphibolites (12.9 ° N, 314.1° E, A95=8.6° ; Rb–Sr age of 2198 ± 172 Ma), and the Kolvitsa peridotites and schists (44.2° N, 232.6° E, A95=5.4° ; assigned magnetization age of 1900 Ma). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within t

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S, 304.8° E, A95=8.3° ; U–Pb age of 2436± 25 Ma), the Voche-Lambina ultramaﬁcs and amphibolites (12.9 ° N, 314.1° E, A95=8.6° ; Rb–Sr age of 2198 ± 172 Ma), and the Kolvitsa peridotites and schists (44.2° N, 232.6° E, A95=5.4° ; assigned magnetization age of 1900 Ma). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within t

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within the Fennoscandian Shield since Jatulian times (2300–2100 Ma). November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

(corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S, 304.8° E, A95=8.3° ; U–Pb age of 2436± 25 Ma), the Voche-Lambina ultramaﬁcs and amphibolites (12.9 ° N, 314.1° E, A95=8.6° ; Rb–Sr age of 2198 ± 172 Ma), and the Kolvitsa peridotites and schists (44.2° N, 232.6° E, A95=5.4° ; assigned magnetization age of 1900 Ma). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within t

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Remanent magnetization was measured with either a cryogenic magnetometer (LETI) or a Schonstedt spinner flux gate magnetometer. He inferred that northward motion of India and its subsequent collision (\"affrontement\") with Asia were responsible for Cenozoic reactivation of earlier structures and for anomalous relief throughout much of Central Asia. Recent work has done much to confirm and quantify these ideas. Crustal shortening within Tibet was attributed to reactivation of earlier structures by Dewey and Burke [1973]. Seismicity and studies of fault traces on satellite imagery confirmed the extent of active deformation within Central Asia [Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975]. From magnetic anomalies in the Indian Ocean, India is estimated to have collided with Eurasia about 55 Ma ago [Patriat and Achache, 1984]. Since then, paleomagnetic and structural evidence suggests that there has been a further convergence of about 2000 km between India and Eurasia [Achache eta/., 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. Still not clear is the style of deformation within Central Asia over the last 55 Ma. Molnar and Tapponnier [1975] drew attention to the importance of strike-slip faulting. Tapponnier et al. He inferred that northward motion of India and its subsequent collision (\"affrontement\") with Asia were responsible for Cenozoic reactivation of earlier structures and for anomalous relief throughout much of Central Asia. Recent work has done much to confirm and quantify these ideas. Crustal shortening within Tibet was attributed to reactivation of earlier structures by Dewey and Burke [1973]. Seismicity and studies of fault traces on satellite imagery confirmed the extent of active deformation within Central Asia [Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975]. From magnetic anomalies in the Indian Ocean, India is estimated to have collided with Eurasia about 55 Ma ago [Patriat and Achache, 1984]. Since then, paleomagnetic and structural evidence suggests that there has been a further convergence of about 2000 km between India and Eurasia [Achache eta/., 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. Still not clear is the style of deformation within Central Asia over the last 55 Ma. Molnar and Tapponnier [1975] drew attention to the importance of strike-slip faulting. Tapponnier et al. The direction of this folding-induced remagnetization yields a new well-defined palcopole position (56øN, 314øE) for south China. Although this palcopole is significantly different from Mesozoic poles reported to date, we infer that a Triassic to Jurassic age is most likely for this remagnetization. SYMONS Department of Geology, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ontario, Canada The Pennsylvanian red beds of the Pictou Group on Prince Edward Island, Canada, retain a stable remanence in hematite that gives a palcomagnetic pole position at 42øN, 131øE (dp=2 ø, din=4ø). Positive conglomerate and contact tests along with dual polarities show that the remanence is primary and of Stephanian age (286-306 Ma). For elongated pole distributions through time, Bingham statistics is more suitable than Fisher statistics. Bingham statistics shows that there is a consistent discordance in the Pennsylvanian to Late Triassic poles from the Appalachian orogenic belt and interior eraton of North America. This discordance is most readily explained by younger partial remagnetization, or possibly complete remagnetization, in many rock units, especially red beds of the interior eraton. Bingham analysis also shows that there is a significant difference between the Colorado Plateau and interior eraton that is mos

is most readily explained by a Laramide 5.5 ø + 2.9 ø clockwise rotation of the plateau relative to the craton. INTRODUCTION The Kiaman (Late Carboniferous-Permian) apparent polar wan- der (APW) path for North America is defined by relatively numer- ous palcopoles [Irving and Irving, 1982; Van der Voo, 1990]. As new poles add to the path's precision, it becomes possible to detect significant differences between the poles from the different terranes to reveal major tectonic events. Estimation of the Colorado Plateau rotation within the North America eraton is one such example [Steiner, 1986, 1988; Bryan and Gordon, 1986, 1990]. We sampled the lowermost Pictou red beds with a well-defined mid Pennsylvanian (Stephanian) age on Prince Edward Island (PEI) to add to the Kiaman APW path for the eraton. These red beds have been studied palcomagnetically by Black [1964] and Roy [1966]. Lacking stratigraphical control, they sampled the entire mid- Pennsylvanian to mid-Early Permian sequence. Also they used alternating field (AF) and low-temperature thermal demagnetiza- tion that are unsuitable for red bed studies by current standards [Roy and Morris, 1983]. Recently, Symons [1990] in a paleomagnetic report of the uppermost Pictou red beds found the Early Permian poles from

ic report of the uppermost Pictou red beds found the Early Permian poles from the northeastern and southwestern North American craton to be significantly different and suggested the possibility of relative motion between the two parts of the craton. This study of the lowermost Pennsylvanian Pictou red beds extends that study. GEOLOGY The Pictou Group on PEI consists of flat-lying red beds that van der Poll [ 1983] subdivided into four upward fining sequences and designated as megacycles I to IV. Each megacycle is 300-400 m thick with a basal pebble conglomerate with clasts consisting of quartzite, rhyolite and other rock types. We sampled only megacy- cle I red beds except for the overlying basal conglomerate and some tilted red beds of lowermost megacycle II (Figure 1). INTRODUCTION Paleomagnetic samples have been obtained by the U.S. Geological Survey from several hundred lava flows erupted from Kilauea, Mauna Loa, and Hualalai volcanoes on the island of Hawaii. The most recent studies were initiated in an attempt to use the history of geomagnetic secular variation recorded by the lava flows to facilitate geologic mapping of the island and thereby aid in the assessment of volcanic hazards [McWilliams et al., 1982; Holcomb et al., 1986]. Within this large inventory of sampled flows are many that have been dated by the radiocarbon (4C) method. We initiated a study of some of the 4C-dated lava flows in order to characterize the variations of geomagnetic intensity throughout Holocene time and to use this information in combination with magnetic directions to enhance the utility of paleomagnetic secular variation as a correlation tool. Several paleointensity studies have been conducted on lava flows on the island of Hawaii, the earliest being per- formed on samples from the Kau and Puna Volcanic Series [Doell and Cox, 1972]. Beca

CHAMPION U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California Paleointensity determinations have been obtained from 22 basaltic lava flows on the island of Hawaii using the Thelliers' method. Radiocarbon dating indicates that these flows erupted at intervals ranging from about 200 to 1000 years, and results of the experiments provide an estimate of broad trends in geomagnetic paleointensity during Holocene time in the vicinity of Hawaii. Most of the samples were obtained from quickly cooled flow margins and, as a consequence, typically contain two titanomag- netite populations. The large nondipole fields that were previously postulated for the vicinity of Hawaii are confirmed, and the present data indicate that they were present from about 5000 years B.P. to perhaps as recently as the past 200 years. The data indicate, however, that these nondipole sources must have been virtually absent between about 12,000 and 5000 years B.P. as they are at the present time. The Antarctic Peninsula (AP) is one of four crustal blocks that define West Antarctica, the others being the Ellsworth- Whitmore Mountains (EWM), Thurston Island-Eights Coast (TI), and Marie Byrd Land (MBL). A Jurassic pole (-155Ma) (124øE, 64øS, A95=7.1 ø, N=10 VGPs) was obtained from the AP block which suggests that the AP block rotated clockwise between -175 and -155 Ma due to significant early opening in the Weddell Sea basin. A new Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic pole (182øE, 74S, A95=5.9 ø, N=6 site mean VGPs) indicates that the AP block was in or near to its present-day position with respect to East Antarctica by -130 Ma. Measurements of the natural reinanent magnetization (NRM) were made using a cryogenic magnetometer or a computerized fluxgate Molspin magnetometer on one or more specimens cut from each core. Pilot samples were progressively demagnetized using step-wise alternating field (AF) or thermal (TH) techniques to determine the best demagnetization procedure for each site. Steps of generally 5 to 10 mT up to a peak of 95 mT were used during AF demagnetization, while steps of generally 50øC up to 500øC and then smaller steps up to a maximum of 660øC were used in thermal demagnetization. Susceptibility measurements were made after each thermal demagnetization step to evaluate mineralogic changes. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) experiments were carried out on representative speciments from the main sample locations. The Antarctic Peninsula (AP) is one of four crustal blocks that define West Antarctica, the others being the Ellsworth- Whitmore Mountains (EWM), Thurston Island-Eights Coast (TI), and Marie Byrd Land (MBL). A Jurassic pole (-155Ma) (124øE, 64øS, A95=7.1 ø, N=10 VGPs) was obtained from the AP block which suggests that the AP block rotated clockwise between -175 and -155 Ma due to significant early opening in the Weddell Sea basin. A new Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic pole (182øE, 74S, A95=5.9 ø, N=6 site mean VGPs) indicates that the AP block was in or near to its present-day position with respect to East Antarctica by -130 Ma. target_context.excerpt: England New paleomagnetic data presented here further constrain the relative motion of the Antarctic Peninsula relative to East Antarctica during the Mesozoic development of the southern ocean basins. The Antarctic Peninsula (AP) is one of four crustal blocks that define West Antarctica, the others being the Ellsworth- Whitmore Mountains (EWM), Thurston Island-Eights Coast (TI), and Marie Byrd Land (MBL). The Antarctic Peninsula (AP) is one of four crustal blocks that define West Antarctica, the others being the Ellsworth- Whitmore Mountains (EWM), Thurston Island-Eights Coast (TI), and Marie Byrd Land (MBL). The Antarctic Peninsula (AP) is one of four crustal blocks that define West Antarctica, the others being the Ellsworth- Whitmore Mountains (EWM), Thurston Island-Eights Coast (TI), and Marie Byrd Land (MBL). A Jurassic pole (-155Ma) (124øE, 64øS, A95=7.1 ø, N=10 VGPs) was obtained from the AP block which suggests that the AP block rotated clockwise between -175 and -155 Ma due to significant early opening in the Weddell Sea basin. A new Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic pole (182øE, 74S, A95=5.9 ø, N=6 site mean VGPs) indicates that the AP block was in or near to its present-day position with respect to East Antarctica by -130 Ma. Between -155 and 130 Ma, counterclockwise rotation of the AP-TI blocks, together with the southward motion of East Gondwanaland, probably resulted in subduction of Weddell Sea ocean floor beneath the southern AP block and initiated the Palmer Land deformational event. Measurements of the natural reinanent magnetization (NRM) were made using a cryogenic magnetometer or a computerized fluxgate Molspin magnetometer on one or more specimens cut from each core. Pilot samples were progressively demagnetized using step-wise alternating field (AF) or thermal (TH) techniques to determine the best demagnetization procedure for each site. Pilot samples were progressively demagnetized using step-wise alternating field (AF) or thermal (TH) techniques to determine the best demagnetization procedure for each site. Steps of generally 5 to 10 mT up to a peak of 95 mT were used during AF demagnetization, while steps of generally 50øC up to 500øC and then smaller steps up to a maximum of 660øC were used in thermal demagnetization. The Antarctic Peninsula (AP) is one of four crustal blocks that define West Antarctica, the others being the Ellsworth- Whitmore Mountains (EWM), Thurston Island-Eights Coast (TI), and Marie Byrd Land (MBL). The sampling sites included fresh looking outcrops except for one site of altered gabbro (\"Deshe\") which was sampled in order to compare an obviously altered rock with the apparently fresh outcrops of the other rock types. All the samples were drilled in the field with a portable drill; orientation of the cores was determined with a sun compass. The friable Deshe was sampled with oriented plastic capsules. The core samples were sliced into 2.5-cm-long specimens to achieve equidimensionality. Several samples were sliced into two specimens, one for alternating field (AF) and the other for thermal treatment. Thin sections were made from cores taken at each sampling site for mineralogical examination. The measurements of remanent magnetizations were made with a three-axis superconducting magnetometer (\"2G Enterprises\"), equipped with a mounted AF demagnetizer, at the Institute for Petroleum Research and Geophysics in Holon. The direction (declination inclination) and intensity (J)of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) were measured first, and then the specimen was subjected to stepwise demagnetization by peak alternating fields of increasing intensity, starting with 5 or 10 mT and going up to 80-100 mT in 5- or 10-mT increments. It is assumed that no tectonic corrections to the data are required since the Precambrian dikes are vertical throughout Mount Timna and relics of Cambrian sediments on top of Mount Timna are essentially horizontal, ruling out post- Cambrian tectonic tilting. Standard orthogonal vector plots [Zijderveld, 1967] are used to illustrate the direction and intensity (J) of the remanent magnetic vector before demagnetization (the NRM) and as demagnetization proceeds (Figure 2). The vector directions were defined as the linear sections that approach the origin and pass a 2 ø linearity test. The mean direction of all the sites in the same rock unit is taken as the characteristic direction of that unit. Several authors determined the late Precambrian position of Africa by combining biogeographic, climatically sensitive lithofacies, and palcomagnetic data: Burrett et al. [1990] and Scotese and Barrett,[1990] showed that the Arabian Peninsula in the late Precambrian was at ~30øS latitude and rotated 90 ø counterclockwise relative to its present position. INTRODUCTION The characteristic remanent magnetization of a rock unit is primarily a result of its thermal history and the formation processes of its constituent magnetic minerals. The use of palcomagnetic data for constraining tectonic models is valid, provided the age of the magnetization is well defined. Magnetic components should be correlated with dated processes of formation or any subsequent modification of the magnetic minerals, before the palcomagnetic data can be correctly interpreted. The present study provides an example of the problems of palcomagnetic interpretation from the Precambrian Arabo Nubian Massif of Arabia and NE Africa and may explain part of the uncertainty noted in the Precambrian apparent polar wander path (APWP) of Africa. PALEoMAGNETIC MEASUREMENTS Magnetic measurements were performed with the CTF three-axis cryogenic magnetometer in the shielded laboratory at the Institut de Physique du Globe in Paris. Alternating field (AF) demagnetization, using a Schonstedt demagnetizer, proved for most part to be ineffective; therefore, most samples were thermally demagnetized using field-free (less than 10 nT) laboratory-built furnaces. Ten to 15 heating steps were made, and the bulk susceptibility of each specimen was monitored after each temperature step in order to check for magnetic mineral changes. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) experiments were carded out on several specimens of different age and rock type. Demagnetization results were plotted as orthogonal vector diagrams and stereographic projections. Upon stepwise thermal demagnetization (12-14 steps), the large majority of samples were very stable and revealed straightforward demagnetization paths. Two sites were excluded due to unstable magnetizations and two more sites were excluded due to large within-site scatter (Table lb). Because the magnetization was so stable, I used only stable endpoint data in the site means with a minimum of three samples per site. Alternating field demagnetization most often gave results similar to thermal demagnetization but occasionally failed to remove partial overprints, so the bulk of the collection was treated with stepwise thermal demagnetization. Analysis of the results revealed three distinct magnetization types. Type 1 samples (n=14) exhibited just one component of magnetization with a steep downward direction, most commonly directed northwest (Figures 7a and 8a). Type 2R (n=11) samples revealed two components of magnetization: a secondary component directed north and steeply downward and a characteristic component directed southeast and upward (Figures 7b and 8b). Type 2N samples (n=9) had two distinct normal components of magnetization: a north and steeply downward directed secondary component followed by a downward directed, but scattered, characteristic component (Figures 7c and 8c). This provides a reasonable upper limit on the age of the Glacier Island rocks and their magnetization. A more tenuous constraint on the age of magnetization is provided by the paleomagnetism of rocks at the Resurrection Peninsula. The remanence there passes a fold test and appears to be primary [Bol eta/., 1992], that is, the magnetization was acquired when the rocks formed. Assuming that the remanence of the rocks at the Resurrection Peninsula and Glacier Island 2R are related, as suggested by their similarities, then the rocks at Glacier Island were probably overprinted soon after they formed, perhaps during accretion. A weak lower bound on the age of overprinting is provided by the paleomagnetism of rocks in southwest Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. Studies there show that all terranes in southern Alaska were in place by about 45 Ma. Upon stepwise thermal demagnetization (12-14 steps), the large majority of samples were very stable and revealed straightforward demagnetization paths. Two sites were excluded due to unstable magnetizations and two more sites were excluded due to large within-site scatter (Table lb). Because the magnetization was so stable, I used only stable endpoint data in the site means with a minimum of three samples per site. Alternating field demagnetization most often gave results similar to thermal demagnetization but occasionally failed to remove partial overprints, so the bulk of the collection was treated with stepwise thermal demagnetization. Analysis of the results revealed three distinct magnetization types. Type 1 samples (n=14) exhibited just one component of magnetization with a steep downward direction, most commonly directed northwest (Figures 7a and 8a). Type 2R (n=11) samples revealed two components of magnetization: a secondary component directed north and steeply downward and a characteristic component directed southeast and upward (Figures 7b and 8b). Type 2N samples (n=9) had two distinct normal components of magnetization: a north and steeply downward directed secondary component followed by a downward directed, but scattered, characteristic component (Figures 7c and 8c). Sixty-two sites (533 samples) of Pliocene volcanic units were collected covering four major rock types with ages of 4.7 to 1.8 Ma. Twenty-two of these sites were from stratigraphic sections of the lower, middle and upper Servilleta Basalt collected in the Rio Grande gorge at two locations 19 km apart. Flows from the lower and middle members in the southern gorge record reversed polarities, while those in Garapata Canyon are normal with an excursion event in the middle of the sequence. Samples were demagnetized using stepwise thermal or alternating field (AF) techniques, with measure- ment of the susceptibility of magnetization using a KLY2 Kappameter after each heating step. The demagnetization results were analyzed using orthogo- nal vector plots [Zijderveld, 1967] and stereographic projec- tion. Linear (planar) demagnetization trajectories were defined by at least three (four) successive data points which were selected by eye, and directions of the linear segments and poles to the planes were calculated using the principal component analysis of Kirschrink [1980]. Where overlap- ping coercivity or blocking temperature (Ta) spectra preven- ted complete separation of the components, great-circle analysis using the method of McFadden aui McElhinny [1988] was carried out on the planar demagnetization trv.jec- tories to establish the direction of the underlying vector. This involves an iterative procedure whereby the maximum likelihood estimate of the endpoint direction within accep- table sector constraints for each great circle can be deter- mined. The great circles are combined with stable endpoint directions, resulting in determination of the best estimate of the mean direction, with the statistics calculated in all cases using Fisher [1953] statistics. The base- ment has undergone low grade metamorphism to lower greenschist facies, and the basin fill comprises a sequence of unmetamorphosed Lower Cambrian to Givetian rocks, unconformably overlain by Westphalian age sedimentary rocks. Nevertheless, paleomagnetism offers the only quantitative tool for determining pre-Mesozoic plate motions and plate configurations. Laurentia occupied the central part of Rodinia, and detailed knowledge of its paleogeographic history during the Vendian will provide the initial framework for the paleogeography of the surrounding landmasses. The Vendian-Early Cambrian (650-540 Ma) portion of the Laurentian apparent polar wander 4625 4626 MEERT ET AL.: PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE CATOCTIN FORMATION path (APWP) is poorly constrained and the subject of recent controversy. The problem in interpreting this segment of the APWP arises from inconsistencies in placing the exact Vendian/Cambrian boundary in a radiometrically calibrated time scale and problems in interpreting disparate poles of similar age. New estimates for the age of the Vendian/Cambrian boundary range between 525 and 560 Ma with the most commonly cited figure of 540 Ma [Link et al., 1992]. A high unblocking-temperature magnetization was isolated in two or more specimens from the remaining 18 sites. We interpret the high unblocking-temperature spectra of these magnetizations to indicate hematite as the dominant carrier of the ChRM. This is consistent with the lithologic descriptions of hematite occurring along crystallographic planes of clinop- tolite [Bell, 1983], the red to orange color of most samples, and the high blocking temperature of the ChRM. Previous paleomagnetic investigators inferred eleven cooling units at Bell Mountain, but insufficient information was given to determine which tuffs had been sampled. This study was undertaken therefore to establish characteristic remanence directions for each tuff sheet. The available paleomagnetic data corroborate the identification of five map units in the Bell Mountain area, but the number of independent observations is too few for the calculation of a reliable paleopole; paleosecular variation of the geomagnetic field would probably not be averaged out. Introduction Upper Cretaceous volcanic rocks of the Roskruge Moun- tains in southeastern Arizona were initially sampled for paleomagnetic study by Vugteveen et al. [1981] to determine a reference paleomagnetic pole (-72 Ma) for the North American plate. This paleopole is of particular interest because few poles are available for North America during the Laramide orogeny and corresponding interval of rapid apparent polar wander. The Roskruge Volcanics include a thick sequence of well-stratified outflow ash flow tuffs, containing many separate cooling units [Bikerman, 1967] that apparently constitute the best preserved section of Cretaceous tuff sheets in Arizona. This section was collected by Vugteveen et al. [1981] at Bell Mountain (Figure 1) on the Tohono O'odham Indian Reservation (access now re- stricted) at 11 sites, each interpreted to represent an individ- ual cooling unit. Our geologic m

These tuffs were interpreted in the field as a single compound cooling unit about 100 m thick, consisting of two gray-brown welded zones (4a and 4b) separated by an intervening nonwelded to partly welded yellow-tan interval. Both units of tuff 4 are compositionally distinctive silicic rhyolite, containing about 10% small broken crystals of quartz and argillized feldspar and characterized by highly fractionated minor element compositions (high Rb, Y, and Nb and low Ba and Sr; Table 2). Sawyer U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, Colorado Abstract. Reconnaissance geologic mapping and petrologic study of the Upper Cretaceous Roskruge Volcanics at Bell Mountain in the Roskruge Mountains, southeastern Arizona, have identified five compositionally distinct ash flow tuffs, including the basal red Viopuli Tuff, which comprise six or seven separate cooling units. Previous paleomagnetic investigators inferred eleven cooling units at Bell Mountain, but insufficient information was given to determine which tuffs had been sampled. This study was undertaken therefore to establish characteristic remanence directions for each tuff sheet. The available paleomagnetic data corroborate the identification of five map units in the Bell Mountain area, but the number of independent observations is too few for the calculation of a reliable paleopole; paleosecular variation of the geomagnetic field would probably not be averaged out. No correlatable tuffs are present at Bell Mountain, so relative vertical axis rotations cannot be determined, although they are probably not large. The absence of regionally correlatable tuf

dependent observations is too few for the calculation of a reliable paleopole; paleosecular variation of the geomagnetic field would probably not be averaged out. No correlatable tuffs are present at Bell Mountain, so relative vertical axis rotations cannot be determined, although they are probably not large. The absence of regionally correlatable tuffs suggests the presence of additional, potentially mineralized, volcanic centers perhaps farther north in the Roskruge Mountains or buried nearby beneath Cenozoic basin fill. Introduction Upper Cretaceous volcanic rocks of the Roskruge Moun- tains in southeastern Arizona were initially sampled for paleomagnetic study by Vugteveen et al. [1981] to determine a reference paleomagnetic pole (-72 Ma) for the North American plate. This paleopole is of particular interest because few poles are available for North America during the Laramide orogeny and corresponding interval of rapid apparent polar wander. The Roskruge Volcanics include a thick sequence of well-stratified outflow ash flow tuffs, containing many separate cooling units [Bikerman, 1967] that apparently constitute the best preserved section of Cretaceous tuff sheets in Arizona. This paleopole is of particular interest because few poles are available for North America during the Laramide orogeny and corresponding interval of rapid apparent polar wander. The Roskruge Volcanics include a thick sequence of well-stratified outflow ash flow tuffs, containing many separate cooling units [Bikerman, 1967] that apparently constitute the best preserved section of Cretaceous tuff sheets in Arizona. This section was collected by Vugteveen et al. [1981] at Bell Mountain (Figure 1) on the Tohono O'odham Indian Reservation (access now re- stricted) at 11 sites, each interpreted to represent an individ- ual cooling unit. Our geologic mapping and petrologic study (Table 1), however, has shown that only five major ash flow compositional units (6 or 7 probable cooling units) are exposed in the Bell Mountain area. Site locations are not given by Vugteveen et al. [1981] in sufficient detail to relate their data to the newly identified tuffs. Also, our studies of the Cretaceous ash flow tuffs and associated caldera sources in the nearby Silver Bell, Tucson, and Sierrita Mountains [Lipman and Sawyer, 1985; Sawyer, 1989; Hagstrum and Sawyer, 1989; Lipman and Fridrich, This paper is not subject

Introduction Jurassic volcanic rocks in southern Arizona have been the subject of previous paleomagnetic investigations to deter- mine cratonic reference poles and the apparent polar wander (APW) path for the North American plate. Assemblages of Upper Jurassic silicic tuffs and flows, including interbedded volcaniclastic conglomerates and sandstones, have been sampled in the Glance Conglomerate of the northern Canelo Hills [Kluth et al., 1982], and similar rocks of Middle Jurassic age have been sampled in Corral Canyon of the Patagonia Mountains [May et al., 1986]. This spread of circa 100 Ma poles demands some explana- tion. Since the sampled units are all plutonic and therefore cooled slowly, the pattern is unlikely to represent paleosecu- lar variation of the Earth's magnetic field. Paleomagnetic results are presented along with several lines of evidence, including a positive tilt test based on the attitude of circa 117 Ma volcanic rocks that the circa 100 Ma rocks intrude, which argue that these results are a representative estimate of the mid-Cretaceous magnetic field in Marie Byrd Land (MBL). Mean paleomagnetic poles were calculated for each of the eight circa 100 Ma locations by averaging the site mean vir- tual geomagnetic poles (VGP). A cluster of poles falls near the coast of MBL including poles from Peden Cliffs (PC), Mount Sinha syenite (SS), Sinha gabbro (SG), and Mount Petras (MP) (Figure 9a). The poles from Cape Burks gabbro (CB), Wilkins Nunatak granite (WG), and the in situ poles from the syenite at Mount Vance (VS) and Mount Langway (LS), however, fall some 30 ø

a syenite (SS), Sinha gabbro (SG), and Mount Petras (MP) (Figure 9a). The poles from Cape Burks gabbro (CB), Wilkins Nunatak granite (WG), and the in situ poles from the syenite at Mount Vance (VS) and Mount Langway (LS), however, fall some 30 ø to either side of the cluster. This spread of circa 100 Ma poles demands some explana- tion. Since the sampled units are all plutonic and therefore cooled slowly, the pattern is unlikely to represent paleosecu- lar variation of the Earth's magnetic field. Also, the angular distance (-65 ø) between the Cape Burks and Mount Vance syenite in situ poles is much too great to be accounted for by apparent polar wander given the very similar ages of the rock units. Therefore given that New Zealand/Campbell Plateau rifted from this margin shortly before 85 Ma [Mayes et aL, 1990], a structural explanation appears likely. Structural control is difficult to achieve in the Ruppert/Hobbs Coast area, which is characterized by isolated igneous outcrops separated by expanses of snow and ice. However, in the Ickes Mountains the syenite intrudes Lower Cretaceous bedded volcanics which outcrop at Mount Vance/Mount LeMasurier. New paleomagnetic results are presented from west central MBL which confirm a high-latitude mid-Cretaceous position for MBL adjacent to the East Antarctic craton. These results are concordant with mid-Cretaceous paleomagnetic results from TI and AP, implying no paleomagnetically resolvable relative motions between the Pacific-bordering blocks of West Antarctica (i.e., all of West Antarctica except EWM; see Figure 1) since the mid-Cretaceous. The West Antarctic mid- Cretaceous paleomagnetic poles are compared with a newly constructed synthetic apparent polar wander path (APWP) for East Antarctica. The poles for MBL, TI, and AP are offset from the East Antarctic APWP, from which it may be concluded that the Pacific West Antarctic blocks have moved with respect to East Antarctica since about 100 Ma. Geologic Background The geologic history of western MBL begins with the depo- sition of a lower Paleozoic turbidite sequence, the Swanson Formation, which was folded and mildly metamorphosed in the Late Ordovician [Adams, 1986]. Mean paleomagnetic poles were calculated for each of the eight circa 100 Ma locations by averaging the site mean vir- tual geomagnetic poles (VGP). A cluster of poles falls near the coast of MBL including poles from Peden Cliffs (PC), Mount Sinha syenite (SS), Sinha gabbro (SG), and Mount Petras (MP) (Figure 9a). The poles from Cape Burks gabbro (CB), Wilkins Nunatak granite (WG), and the in situ poles from the syenite at Mount Vance (VS) and Mount Langway (LS), however, fall some 30 ø

a syenite (SS), Sinha gabbro (SG), and Mount Petras (MP) (Figure 9a). The poles from Cape Burks gabbro (CB), Wilkins Nunatak granite (WG), and the in situ poles from the syenite at Mount Vance (VS) and Mount Langway (LS), however, fall some 30 ø to either side of the cluster. This spread of circa 100 Ma poles demands some explana- tion. Since the sampled units are all plutonic and therefore cooled slowly, the pattern is unlikely to represent paleosecu- lar variation of the Earth's magnetic field. Also, the angular distance (-65 ø) between the Cape Burks and Mount Vance syenite in situ poles is much too great to be accounted for by apparent polar wander given the very similar ages of the rock units. Therefore given that New Zealand/Campbell Plateau rifted from this margin shortly before 85 Ma [Mayes et aL, 1990], a structural explanation appears likely. Structural control is difficult to achieve in the Ruppert/Hobbs Coast area, which is characterized by isolated igneous outcrops separated by expanses of snow and ice. However, in the Ickes Mountains the syenite intrudes Lower Cretaceous bedded volcanics which outcrop at Mount Vance/Mount LeMasurier. [Patriat and Achache, 1984], the regional tectonics appear to have resulted from indentation of Asia by India [Argand, 1924; Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975], with a bulk N-S shortening of about 2000 km [Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. n Tertiary and Cretaceous data available for the area shows that rotations have occurred since the Miocene. Little or no paleomagnetic rotations are observed in the ranges bordering the northern and western parts of the depression. Paleomagnetic and structural data suggest that block rotations in the Tadjik depression are associated with indentation of the Pareits into stable Asia. At a larger scale, observed rotations are compatible with a model of regional sinistral wrenching, along a strip running from the Gulf of Oman to Lake Baikal. Introduction Central Asia provides a remarkable example of large-scale active intracontinental deformation. Over the last 55 m.y. [Patriat and Achache, 1984], the regional tectonics appear to have resulted from indentation of Asia by India [Argand, 1924; Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975], with a bulk N-S shortening of about 2000 km [Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. Among the various kinematic models [e.g., Dewey and Burke, 1973; Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Houseman and England, 1986, 1993; Cobbold and Davy, 1988; Davy and Cobbold, 1988; Dewey eta/., 1989; Avouac and Tapponnier, 1992; Le Pichon et al., 1992] a key point, but a controversial one, is the partitioning between crustal thickening and strike-slip motions alo

Recent paleomagnetic studies have consistently revealed clockwise rotations of up to 40 ø in Cretaceous rocks from eastern Tibet and southwest China [Otofuji eta/., 1990; Huang and Opdike, 1992; Funahara et al., 1993], and counterclockwise rotations of up to 20 ø in Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of intermontane basins of the Tien-Shan [Thomas eta/., 1993; Bazhenov, 1993]. n Tertiary and Cretaceous data available for the area shows that rotations have occurred since the Miocene. Little or no paleomagnetic rotations are observed in the ranges bordering the northern and western parts of the depression. Paleomagnetic and structural data suggest that block rotations in the Tadjik depression are associated with indentation of the Pareits into stable Asia. At a larger scale, observed rotations are compatible with a model of regional sinistral wrenching, along a strip running from the Gulf of Oman to Lake Baikal. Introduction Central Asia provides a remarkable example of large-scale active intracontinental deformation. Over the last 55 m.y. [Patriat and Achache, 1984], the regional tectonics appear to have resulted from indentation of Asia by India [Argand, 1924; Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975], with a bulk N-S shortening of about 2000 km [Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. Among the various kinematic models [e.g., Dewey and Burke, 1973; Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Houseman and England, 1986, 1993; Cobbold and Davy, 1988; Davy and Cobbold, 1988; Dewey eta/., 1989; Avouac and Tapponnier, 1992; Le Pichon et al., 1992] a key point, but a controversial one, is the partitioning between crustal thickening and strike-slip motions alo

Recent paleomagnetic studies have consistently revealed clockwise rotations of up to 40 ø in Cretaceous rocks from eastern Tibet and southwest China [Otofuji eta/., 1990; Huang and Opdike, 1992; Funahara et al., 1993], and counterclockwise rotations of up to 20 ø in Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of intermontane basins of the Tien-Shan [Thomas eta/., 1993; Bazhenov, 1993]. However, they are shallower by about 30 ø than the inclination predicted from the reference apparent polar wander path. n Tertiary and Cretaceous data available for the area shows that rotations have occurred since the Miocene. Little or no paleomagnetic rotations are observed in the ranges bordering the northern and western parts of the depression. Paleomagnetic and structural data suggest that block rotations in the Tadjik depression are associated with indentation of the Pareits into stable Asia. At a larger scale, observed rotations are compatible with a model of regional sinistral wrenching, along a strip running from the Gulf of Oman to Lake Baikal. Introduction Central Asia provides a remarkable example of large-scale active intracontinental deformation. Over the last 55 m.y. [Patriat and Achache, 1984], the regional tectonics appear to have resulted from indentation of Asia by India [Argand, 1924; Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975], with a bulk N-S shortening of about 2000 km [Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. n Tertiary and Cretaceous data available for the area shows that rotations have occurred since the Miocene. Little or no paleomagnetic rotations are observed in the ranges bordering the northern and western parts of the depression. Paleomagnetic and structural data suggest that block rotations in the Tadjik depression are associated with indentation of the Pareits into stable Asia. At a larger scale, observed rotations are compatible with a model of regional sinistral wrenching, along a strip running from the Gulf of Oman to Lake Baikal. Introduction Central Asia provides a remarkable example of large-scale active intracontinental deformation. Over the last 55 m.y. [Patriat and Achache, 1984], the regional tectonics appear to have resulted from indentation of Asia by India [Argand, 1924; Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975], with a bulk N-S shortening of about 2000 km [Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. Among the various kinematic models [e.g., Dewey and Burke, 1973; Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Houseman and England, 1986, 1993; Cobbold and Davy, 1988; Davy and Cobbold, 1988; Dewey eta/., 1989; Avouac and Tapponnier, 1992; Le Pichon et al., 1992] a key point, but a controversial one, is the partitioning between crustal thickening and strike-slip motions alo

Recent paleomagnetic studies have consistently revealed clockwise rotations of up to 40 ø in Cretaceous rocks from eastern Tibet and southwest China [Otofuji eta/., 1990; Huang and Opdike, 1992; Funahara et al., 1993], and counterclockwise rotations of up to 20 ø in Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of intermontane basins of the Tien-Shan [Thomas eta/., 1993; Bazhenov, 1993]. The Tadjik depression, which lies South of the Tien-Shan and West of the Pareits (Figure 2), is part of the Oman-Baikal sinistral wrench zone [Cobbold and Davy, 1988]. n Tertiary and Cretaceous data available for the area shows that rotations have occurred since the Miocene. Little or no paleomagnetic rotations are observed in the ranges bordering the northern and western parts of the depression. Paleomagnetic and structural data suggest that block rotations in the Tadjik depression are associated with indentation of the Pareits into stable Asia. At a larger scale, observed rotations are compatible with a model of regional sinistral wrenching, along a strip running from the Gulf of Oman to Lake Baikal. Introduction Central Asia provides a remarkable example of large-scale active intracontinental deformation. Over the last 55 m.y. [Patriat and Achache, 1984], the regional tectonics appear to have resulted from indentation of Asia by India [Argand, 1924; Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975], with a bulk N-S shortening of about 2000 km [Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. Among the various kinematic models [e.g., Dewey and Burke, 1973; Achache and Courtillot, 1984; Houseman and England, 1986, 1993; Cobbold and Davy, 1988; Davy and Cobbold, 1988; Dewey eta/., 1989; Avouac and Tapponnier, 1992; Le Pichon et al., 1992] a key point, but a controversial one, is the partitioning between crustal thickening and strike-slip motions alo

Recent paleomagnetic studies have consistently revealed clockwise rotations of up to 40 ø in Cretaceous rocks from eastern Tibet and southwest China [Otofuji eta/., 1990; Huang and Opdike, 1992; Funahara et al., 1993], and counterclockwise rotations of up to 20 ø in Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks of intermontane basins of the Tien-Shan [Thomas eta/., 1993; Bazhenov, 1993]. The Sherman Granite is transitional between true granite and quartz monzonite and is petrologically and compositionally similar to Middle Proterozoic granites exposed elsewhere in Colorado [Tweto, 1987; Geist et al., 1989]. Sherman Granite from the south- ern Laramie Range is pink to red, coarse-grained, equigranular to porphyritic granite that contains perthific microcline, quartz, sodic plagioclase, biotite, and hornblende [Geist et al., 1989]. Locally, microcline is mantled by plagioclase, resulting in a distinctive rapa- kivi texture [Zielinski et al., 1981]. Accessory phases include ilmenite, magnetite, apatite, sphene, and zircon [Geist et al., 1989]. In the ring dike complex, composite zones of quartz monzonite and diorite and small bodies of andesite and dacite are also present [Eggler, 1968]. The Sherman Granite was intruded by noahwest trending mafic dikes, and both the Sherman Granite and dikes are cut by the Log Cabin batholith. The Laramie anorthosite complex, Sherman Gran- ite, mafic dikes, and Log Cabin batholith are part of the Berthoud Plutonic Suite in Colorado and are related to a major belt of Middle Proterozoic magmatism that extended 4800 km from Labrador southwestward across the North American continent to Calif

The Sherman Granite is transitional between true granite and quartz monzonite and is petrologically and compositionally similar to Middle Proterozoic granites exposed elsewhere in Colorado [Tweto, 1987; Geist et al., 1989]. Sherman Granite from the south- ern Laramie Range is pink to red, coarse-grained, equigranular to porphyritic granite that contains perthific microcline, quartz, sodic plagioclase, biotite, and hornblende [Geist et al., 1989]. Locally, microcline is mantled by plagioclase, resulting in a distinctive rapa- kivi texture [Zielinski et al., 1981]. Accessory phases include ilmenite, magnetite, apatite, sphene, and zircon [Geist et al., 1989]. In the ring dike complex, composite zones of quartz monzonite and diorite and small bodies of andesite and dacite are also present [Eggler, 1968]. The Sherman Granite was intruded by noahwest trending mafic dikes, and both the Sherman Granite and dikes are cut by the Log Cabin batholith. The Laramie anorthosite complex, Sherman Gran- ite, mafic dikes, and Log Cabin batholith are part of the Berthoud Plutonic Suite in Colorado and are related to a major belt of Middle Proterozoic magmatism that extended 4800 km from Labrador southwestward across the North American continent to Calif

The Sherman Granite is transitional between true granite and quartz monzonite and is petrologically and compositionally similar to Middle Proterozoic granites exposed elsewhere in Colorado [Tweto, 1987; Geist et al., 1989]. Sherman Granite from the south- ern Laramie Range is pink to red, coarse-grained, equigranular to porphyritic granite that contains perthific microcline, quartz, sodic plagioclase, biotite, and hornblende [Geist et al., 1989]. Locally, microcline is mantled by plagioclase, resulting in a distinctive rapa- kivi texture [Zielinski et al., 1981]. Accessory phases include ilmenite, magnetite, apatite, sphene, and zircon [Geist et al., 1989]. In the ring dike complex, composite zones of quartz monzonite and diorite and small bodies of andesite and dacite are also present [Eggler, 1968]. The Sherman Granite was intruded by noahwest trending mafic dikes, and both the Sherman Granite and dikes are cut by the Log Cabin batholith. The Laramie anorthosite complex, Sherman Gran- ite, mafic dikes, and Log Cabin batholith are part of the Berthoud Plutonic Suite in Colorado and are related to a major belt of Middle Proterozoic magmatism that extended 4800 km from Labrador southwestward across the North American continent to Calif
